title: Delta Confirms Return to Singapore as Airline Plots Biggest Asia Expansion in a Decade
excerpt: Delta's chief commercial officer says the carrier will resume Singapore flights and shift long-haul growth from saturated European routes to the Pacific.
body:
• Delta Air Lines chief commercial officer Joe Esposito confirmed the airline will resume flights to Singapore, likely from its Seattle hub, after last serving the route in 2019.
  • The Singapore return is part of Delta's largest Asia expansion in over a decade, following its resumed Hong Kong service, new Manila route, and a surprise return to Tokyo Narita.
  • Delta is shifting long-haul growth away from Europe, where executives say the airline's network is near capacity, toward high-demand Pacific and Southeast Asian markets.
  • The expansion will be powered by Airbus A350-1000 aircraft, Delta's incoming flagship designed for flights exceeding 15 hours.

Singapore Confirmed

Delta Air Lines is headed back to Singapore. Joe Esposito, the airline's chief commercial officer, confirmed the return in an interview this week, seven years after Delta last served the Southeast Asian hub via Tokyo.

"We're going to be back in Singapore," Esposito said, signaling what aviation analysts have anticipated since Delta began quietly rebuilding its Pacific network earlier this year.

While no route has been formally announced, Esposito ruled out nonstop service from Los Angeles, suggesting that Seattle-Tacoma International Airport — Delta's Pacific-facing West Coast hub — is the leading candidate. United Airlines is currently the only U.S. carrier operating nonstop flights to Singapore's Changi Airport.

"Asia, to us, is where we have opportunity for growth in the future."

— Joe Esposito, Chief Commercial Officer, Delta Air Lines

A Pacific Pivot

The Singapore return is one piece of a broader strategic shift that marks Delta's most significant Asia expansion since it absorbed Northwest Airlines' sprawling Pacific network in 2008.

This summer alone, Delta resumed flights to Hong Kong from Los Angeles for the first time since 2018 and announced a new nonstop route to Manila. Last week, the airline revealed a return to Tokyo's Narita Airport, where Northwest once operated a full overseas hub.

The carrier is also working to connect its Los Angeles and New York JFK hubs directly to Seoul Incheon, the base of its joint venture partner Korean Air, which provides connecting access to roughly 80 Asian destinations.

The expansion is deliberate — and directional. Delta executives view their European route network as approaching saturation after years of aggressive transatlantic buildout alongside partners Air France, KLM, and Virgin Atlantic.

"There's still unique destinations to fly to," Esposito said of Europe. "But we have really great access already. We don't have as much access to Asia."

The A350-1000 Factor

Delta's Pacific ambitions are tightly linked to its incoming fleet of Airbus A350-1000 aircraft, the carrier's new flagship. The widebody jet offers the range to operate routes exceeding 15 hours nonstop and will feature a higher proportion of Delta One Suites and Premium Select seats than current configurations.

Delta has 20 A350-1000s on order, alongside six remaining A350-900 deliveries. The airline's A330neo fleet will handle medium-haul Pacific routes, including an expanded Hawaii operation launching in late 2026.

The fleet strategy mirrors what worked for Northwest, but with a critical difference. Northwest's Asian network was anchored by a hub in Tokyo that required connections; Delta will operate direct flights from the U.S. mainland.

"When you think about where we were the past 20 years, they had a great Pacific network but really didn't have the strength on the West Coast to launch from," Esposito said. "Now we've got great launching platforms."

Beyond the Pacific

Delta's international push extends beyond Asia. The airline will launch nonstop service to Riyadh in October, becoming the first U.S. carrier to offer direct flights to Saudi Arabia. It also announced this week a new Austin-to-Paris route starting in 2027.

But the Pacific is where the big bets are concentrated. Delta sees its dual West Coast hubs at LAX and Seattle-Tacoma as natural gateways to markets that United has dominated among U.S. carriers.

What It Means for Travelers

For Indian diaspora travelers in the United States, Delta's Singapore return and broader Asia expansion add another nonstop option for reaching Southeast Asia — a region that serves as a common transit point for flights to India's southern cities. More U.S.-Asia competition from Delta could also put downward pressure on fares on routes where United has operated without a direct American competitor.
